text: therapy have been given intravenous co-trimox- azole or clindamycin with oral pyrimethamine.8 Adjunc- tive corticosteroids may be given occasionally for treat- ment of a mass effect associated with focal lesions or oedema, but should be stopped as soon as possible because of their immunosuppressant effect. Anticonvulsants should be given to patients with a history of seizures.8 Acute treatment is ideally continued for 6 weeks, or for longer if disease is extensive or response is incomplete. Patients who have successfully completed a 6-week course of acute therapy should be given chronic mainte- nance therapy, which should ideally be with pyrimeth- amine plus sulfadiazine and folinic acid, but alternatives are pyrimethamine plus clindamycin and folinic acid, or atovaquone, with or without pyrimethamine and folinic acid.8 Chronic maintenance therapy should be lifelong un- less immune reconstitution occurs because of antiretro- viral therapy, in which case consideration may be given to stopping prophylaxis. It should, however, be restarted if the CD4+ T lymphocyte count falls to below 200 cells/mi- crolitre.8 A systematic review9 of the treatment of women during pregnancy has involved small studies with variations in period of gestation, duration of follow-up, and other as- pects of methodology, making comparison of data prob- lematical; consequently the evidence is inconclusive as to whether treatment is effective in preventing fetal infection or overt neonatal disease. If treatment is given, pyrimeth- amine should not be used to treat primary toxoplasmosis during the first trimester of pregnancy in immunocompe- tent patients. Spiramycin has been used throughout the first trimester but, although it reduces the risk of congenital transmission, it does not readily penetrate the cerebrospi- nal space and does not prevent toxoplasmic encephalitis in immunocompromised women. After the first trimester py- rimethamine may be given with sulfadiazine and folinic acid and, when there is evidence of placental or fetal infec- tion, this treatment may be alternated with courses of spiramycin until term. In neonates with congenital toxo- plasmosis, the preferred treatment is pyrimethamine to- gether with sulfadiazine and folinic acid.7 Infants without HIV infection should be treated for 12 months. In infants with mild toxoplasmosis, some experts recommend alter- nating pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with spiramycin on a monthly basis from months 7 to 12, in order to reduce the risk of bone marrow suppression. However, infants with HIV infection and moderate to severe toxoplasmosis should receive the full 12-month regimen of pyrimeth- amine-sulfadiazine.7 Longer courses of treatment may be given in cases of extensive disease.
